implementation_notes: Play is the dispatcher (a compiled conf/routes table mapping GET /orders/:id to a controller method), the Action block is the worker (it calls the injected service and builds the view parameters), and Ok(views.html.orders.show(order)) renders a Twirl template compiled from app/views/orders/show.scala.html - so view names are checked by the compiler and @-decorated helper templates fill the view-helper role. What replaces the classic structure is the router plus compiled templates; a runtime-string dispatcher is unnecessary here, and the functional stack replaces templates with typed HTML values (see the http4s-scalatags variant).
code_sketch:
def show(id: Long) = Action { implicit request =>
  val order = orderService.find(id)        // worker services the request
  Ok(views.html.orders.show(order))        // compiled Twirl view, checked at build time
}
pitfalls: Blocking calls (JDBC) inside Action run on Play's default execution context and starve it; move them to the blocking pool or a dedicated dispatcher.
Twirl templates are compiled, so template errors surface at build time but compile times grow with every template, and changing a template's parameters breaks all callers at once.
The action passes arbitrary values to the template; without case-class view models the contract drifts into tuples or maps that nothing checks.

variants.name: http4s with scalatags (typed HTML values, no template files)
variants.implementation_notes: Functional realization: HttpRoutes.of[IO] { case GET -> Root / "orders" / id => ... } is the dispatcher as a partial function, the body is the worker running its effects in IO, and scalatags builds the HTML as a typed value - html("<!DOCTYPE html>")(body(h1(order.id))) - instead of rendering a template, so the "view" is code the compiler checks and there is no template directory at all. Choose it when the stack is already cats-effect/http4s and views are small components; Play with Twirl stays better for template-heavy HTML authored by people who do not write Scala.
pitfalls: Building markup in code removes template hot-reload: every copy change recompiles and redeploys the service.
Tag trees are expressions - a large page becomes one large expression, so extract functions or components early to keep it readable.
scalatags support lives in the separate http4s-scalatags module and import (org.http4s.scalatags._); without it the Ok(page) needs a plain text encoder.
